title: There is and there isn't
goal: Say that something exists or that you have it, negate it with *wala*, and recognize when *may* turns into *mayroon*.
bekal: negate existence and possession with *wala*, not with *hindi*
combine *may* with short pronouns: *may kotse ako*, *mayroon akong kotse*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Sa boarding house
dialogs.intro: Budi is looking around a new rented room. Aling Nena explains what's in it.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Mayroon po bang aircon sa kwarto?
lines.id: Is there an air conditioner in the room, ma'am?

lines.speaker: Aling Nena:
lines.text: Wala. Bentilador lang. Pero malamig dito sa gabi.
lines.id: No. Just a fan. But it's cool here at night.
lines.literal: none. fan only. but cold here in night.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ayos lang po. May kusina ba kayo?
lines.id: That's fine, ma'am. Do you have a kitchen?
lines.literal: okay just ma'am. there-is kitchen [question] you-all?

lines.speaker: Aling Nena:
lines.text: Mayroon, sa baba. Pero walang gas ngayon.
lines.id: Yes, downstairs. But there's no gas right now.
lines.literal: there-is, in below. but no-gas now.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: May tindahan po ba malapit dito?
lines.id: Is there a shop near here, ma'am?

lines.speaker: Aling Nena:
lines.text: Marami! May sari-sari store sa kanto.
lines.id: Plenty! There's a sari-sari store on the corner.
lines.literal: many! there-is sari-sari store on corner.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Salamat po. Wala na po akong tanong.
lines.id: Thank you, ma'am. I don't have any more questions.
lines.literal: thanks ma'am. none now ma'am I-that question.

lines.speaker: Aling Nena:
lines.text: Sige. May susi ka na ba?
lines.id: Good. Do you have a key yet?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Wala pa po. Bukas na lang po.
lines.id: Not yet, ma'am. Tomorrow will do.
lines.literal: none yet ma'am. tomorrow now just ma'am.

notes: **May does two jobs at once**: "there is" (existence) and "have" (possession). *May wifi dito* = there's wifi here. *May kotse ako* = I have a car. Tagalog doesn't feel the need to separate them, and after a few days neither will you.

**Mayroon is may that can stand alone.** *May* always needs a noun right behind it; if a particle gets in the way (*ba*, *po*, *ka*), the form switches to *mayroon*: *May aircon ba?* is fine, but *Mayroon po bang aircon?* is neater. And as a one-word answer only *mayroon* works: *Mayroon.* (There is.)
**Wala negates both.** This is important: existence and possession are **not** negated with *hindi*. *Hindi may kotse ako* is totally wrong; the correct form is *wala akong kotse*.
**Walang gas** shows the linker you learned in unit 3: *wala* + *-ng* + noun. Likewise *walang tanong*, *walang pera*, *walang problema*.
**Wala pa means "not yet"**, while *wala na* means "no longer". These two small particles reverse the direction of time, and both are covered fully in unit 14.

**The sari-sari store** is a Philippine social institution, not just a shop. A tiny neighborhood store in front of someone's house, selling everything in sachet sizes — and usually also the spot where people stand chatting all afternoon. *Sari-sari* itself means "assorted", a word that also lives in Malay.
**Kanto** (from Spanish *canto*) means a street corner. *Sa kanto* is one of the most common directions you'll hear in the Philippines, because so much is located on corners.

**Aircon** from *air conditioner*, shortened in a typically Filipino way. The same clipping gives *ref* (fridge) and *CR* (bathroom, from *comfort room*) — English-based words that aren't used like that anywhere except the Philippines.
**Bukas na lang** = "tomorrow will do". The *na lang* combination marks a decision replacing an earlier plan, much like "…just do it tomorrow instead" in English.

grammars.title: May, mayroon, wala — which one to use
body: The three state the same thing from different sides. What decides the form isn't the meaning, but **what stands after it**.
after: *Meron* is *mayroon* shortened in conversation. You'll hear it far more often than the long form; in writing, still use *mayroon*.
Notice the linker that appears as soon as there's a pronoun: *mayroon **akong** kotse*, *wala **akong** pera*. Pronoun and noun are joined with *-ng* — just the unit 3 rule.
⚠️ The question is *May … ba?* or *Mayroon bang …?* Don't combine them: *May bang kotse?* is wrong.

grammars.title: Wala versus hindi
body: Tagalog has three words for "no/not", and choosing the wrong one is the beginner mistake that shows fastest.
after: The short rule: if the positive sentence uses *may* or *nasa*, the negative is **always** *wala*. Otherwise, *hindi*.
*Huwag* is only for forbidding, and is often shortened to *wag* in conversation and texting: *Wag ka nang umiyak.*
The "no" answer to a *may…?* question is also *wala*, not *hindi*: — *May pera ka ba?* — *Wala.*

sections.title: What you find in a Filipino home

blocks.text: Notice *walis* (broom) and *sabon* (soap) — if you know Malay or Spanish you may recognize *sabon* (cf. Spanish *jabón*, Malay *sabun*) right away. *Tubig* (water) is a typically Philippine word, related to Malay *tubir* only distantly.

blocks.title: English words you must use
items: *CR* for the bathroom. Asking *Nasaan ang banyo?* will be understood, but *Nasaan po ang CR?* is what people actually say.
*Ref*, *aircon*, *cellphone*, *load* (phone credit), *sachet*, *tricycle*. For modern objects, Tagalog is truly English-speaking.

blocks.text: This question pattern you'll use every day — in shops, boarding houses, restaurants, terminals.

*Wala na* and *mayroon pa* use two opposing particles: *na* means "already", *pa* means "still". The combinations are very productive — *wala na* (none left), *meron pa* (still some), *wala pa* (none yet), *meron na* (there already is).

exercises.prompt: Fill in may, mayroon or wala.
Negate the following sentences. Example: May kotse ako. → Wala akong kotse.
Put the words in the right order.
